findings: The prompt fails to treat verbal complexes (negation, resultatives, verb‑object compounds, auxiliaries/aspect markers) as atomic for entailment: it ranks cuts that orphan or split predicates too highly.

The prompt overweights protecting multi-character names/transliterations/technical tokens and therefore shifts cuts to avoid splitting them, often creating isolated punctuation, reporting verbs, or short predicate fragments that become unentailed.

diagnosis.why: The prompt now avoids cutting inside verbal complexes (C4) so predicates and their punctuation tend to stay intact—helpful for long-latency examples—but the new C3 rule for splitting multi-token spans was applied too broadly, causing over‑splitting (even into single characters) and isolating punctuation/quotes; that fragmentation shows up as losses in the ≤5 and ≤7 bins despite gains at very short (≤3) and very long (≤99) latencies.
diagnosis.lesson: Narrow the multi-token-splitting rule so it only splits true multi-token names when necessary and never breaks ordinary words or isolates punctuation/quotes; keep the verbal-complex protection but avoid applying splitting heuristics that fragment short/medium pieces.
